At A the ball is thrown horizontally, so its vertical velocity is 0; at C the velocity is also horizontal, so its vertical velocity is again 0. Let the vertical velocity at B be v_By. Then from A to B the velocity change is purely vertical with magnitude |v_By-0|=|v_By|. From B to C the velocity change is also purely vertical with magnitude |0-v_By|=|v_By|. Therefore the two velocity-change magnitudes are equal.

method.method_draft: Use geometric displacement ratios and constant-acceleration kinematics. Set horizontal velocity as v0, downward as positive. From A to B, acceleration is g, so if the time is t, the velocity change magnitude is g t. Because A, B, C are collinear and AB=2BC, the horizontal displacement from B to C is half that from A to B; since horizontal speed is unchanged, the time from B to C is t/2. Also the vertical displacement from B to C is half that from A to B. Let the net vertical acceleration in the electric-field region be a. Then y_AB=(1/2)gt^2, while y_BC=(gt)(t/2)+(1/2)a(t/2)^2. Set y_BC=y_AB/2 to get a=-2g. Thus the velocity change magnitude from B to C is |a|(t/2)=2g·t/2=gt, equal to that from A to B.
